events.title: The May 2024 Gannon geomagnetic superstorm
events.summary: A sequence of Earth-directed coronal mass ejections produced the first G5 geomagnetic storm in more than two decades, with global aurora, major upper-atmosphere changes, and widespread impacts to navigation and spacecraft operations.
events.synopsis: This is the strongest geomagnetic storm in more than twenty years, and the first that a satellite-dependent world experienced in full. A sequence of coronal mass ejections from one very large active region arrived in close succession over 10-11 May 2024, producing G5 conditions, aurora at latitudes that almost never see it, and a measurable swelling of the upper atmosphere. The replay tracks that swelling, because the density change is what most spacecraft operators actually felt.
events.lesson: Follow the causal chain without collapsing it: flare photons arrived first, ejecta and energetic particles followed, then the magnetosphere, ionosphere, and neutral thermosphere responded on their own timescales.

impacts.text: The first G5 (extreme) geomagnetic storm since 2003, and the strongest in more than two decades.
impacts.attribution: NOAA SWPC

impacts.text: Aurora was visible at unusually low latitudes worldwide, including across much of the continental United States.
impacts.attribution: NASA event overview

impacts.text: Precision GPS guidance used by farm equipment was degraded across parts of North America during planting season.
impacts.attribution: Contemporary reporting and equipment-dealer advisories; NOAA SWPC storm advisories

impacts.text: The upper atmosphere expanded enough to raise drag sharply on satellites in low orbit. Roughly half the active spacecraft in low orbit manoeuvred at once, most of it automatic station-keeping, and while they were moving the volume of unplanned motion made collision screening impracticable.
impacts.attribution: Parker and Linares, satellite drag analysis of the May 2024 storm (2024)

impacts.text: Grid operators recorded high geomagnetically induced currents and isolated equipment problems — transformers, voltage-support plant, line breakers, harmonic filters — and took protective measures. There was no major outage.
impacts.attribution: NERC after-action review of the May 2024 geomagnetic disturbance

milestones.title: Active region erupts
milestones.description: Multiple strong flares and Earth-directed CMEs leave the Sun. X-ray and EUV photons reach Earth in about eight minutes; the bulk ejecta is still days away.

milestones.title: First shock reaches L1
milestones.description: Upstream monitors observe a sudden increase in solar-wind speed and pressure. The warning time from L1 to Earth is measured in tens of minutes, depending on speed.

milestones.title: Dayside compression
milestones.description: The stronger solar-wind pressure compresses the dayside magnetopause. Southward IMF supports magnetic reconnection and transfers energy into the system.

milestones.title: G5 conditions
milestones.description: Geomagnetic activity reaches the extreme G5 level. Auroral currents intensify and expand equatorward while the ionosphere becomes highly structured.

milestones.title: Thermospheric response
milestones.description: Energy deposited high in the atmosphere raises neutral temperature and density. LEO spacecraft experience additional drag; TEC disturbances affect GNSS signals.

milestones.title: Uneven recovery
milestones.description: Different parts of the geospace system recover at different rates. Radiation belts, thermospheric density, and ionospheric structure do not simply return to normal together.

replay.title: The air at 480 km, as a spacecraft felt it and as the forecast called it

measured.detail: accelerometer-derived density at 483 km, averaged over one revolution

model.label: WAM-IPE, forecast
model.detail: the same model field read at Swarm-C's own latitude, longitude and altitude

map.label: Density at 400 km, relative to the same place on the quiet day

driver.label: SML
driver.name: Westward auroral electrojet
driver.citation: Auroral electrojet indices from SuperMAG (Gjerloev, J. W., 2012, J. Geophys. Res., doi:10.1029/2012JA017683). We gratefully acknowledge the SuperMAG collaborators and the ground magnetometer operators whose stations make these indices possible.
driver.usage: Derived visualisation, published with citation. The underlying SuperMAG series is not redistributed.

provenance.measured: Swarm-C thermospheric density (ESA product DNSCACC_2_, processed by TU Delft), derived from the spacecraft's calibrated non-gravitational accelerations at ten-second cadence and averaged here over one full revolution.
provenance.model: NOAA SWPC Whole Atmosphere Model-Ionosphere Plasmasphere Electrodynamics (WAM-IPE) Forecast System, fixed-height density product, archived hourly.
provenance.cycleRule: Every model frame is the freshest cycle covering its valid time, at zero to five hours of lead. WAM runs four cycles a day; the whisker at each six-hour boundary is the PREVIOUS cycle's forecast for that same moment. The two are never averaged, because the average is a trajectory neither run produced.
provenance.driver: Auroral electrojet indices from SuperMAG (Gjerloev, J. W., 2012, J. Geophys. Res., doi:10.1029/2012JA017683). We gratefully acknowledge the SuperMAG collaborators and the ground magnetometer operators whose stations make these indices possible.
provenance.method: Both curves are the same quantity at the same point: mass density, sampled at Swarm-C's latitude, longitude and altitude, averaged over the same revolution. The model field is read trilinearly from WAM's 4 x 2 degree, 10 km grid. Each curve is divided by its own 9 May mean, so the comparison is of shape and amplitude and does not depend on either source's absolute calibration.
provenance.limitation: The model curve is a forecast, not an analysis: WAM-IPE assimilates no thermospheric density, so nothing here corrects it toward the spacecraft. The measured curve is one spacecraft on one orbit plane at two fixed local times, not a global average. The map is model output at a single altitude and carries no measurement anywhere in it.
provenance.drag: Atmospheric drag is proportional to density, so the ratio on this axis is also the ratio of the drag force on anything at that altitude. Turning that into a decay rate needs a ballistic coefficient this page does not have, so the ratio is quoted and the metres per day are not.

events.title: The February 2022 Starlink loss
events.summary: A modest geomagnetic storm raised neutral density near the very low deployment altitude of a newly launched Starlink batch. Thirty-eight of forty-nine spacecraft ultimately reentered.
events.synopsis: This is the clearest case in the record of space weather destroying spacecraft through the air rather than through electronics. SpaceX launched forty-nine Starlink satellites on 3 February 2022 into a deliberately low insertion orbit, around 210 km, where a satellite is meant to check out and then climb. A geomagnetic storm that barely registered on the storm scale warmed and expanded the upper atmosphere underneath them, and the thicker air pulled them down faster than they could climb. The chart follows the orbits themselves.
events.lesson: This is the cleanest case for separating ionospheric plasma effects from neutral thermospheric drag: the spacecraft were lost primarily because the neutral atmosphere expanded and increased aerodynamic drag.

impacts.text: Thirty-eight of the forty-nine satellites launched reentered the atmosphere within days. Eleven reached their operational orbit.
impacts.attribution: Fang and others, NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center analysis of the event

impacts.text: Atmospheric density at the deployment altitude rose sharply during a storm rated only minor on the geomagnetic scale.
impacts.attribution: NOAA-authored study of the event

impacts.text: The satellites were commanded edge-on to reduce drag; it was not enough to overcome the increase.
impacts.attribution: SpaceX statement of 8 February 2022

impacts.text: No debris resulted. The spacecraft reentered and burned up, which is the outcome the low insertion altitude is chosen to guarantee.
impacts.attribution: SpaceX statement of 8 February 2022

milestones.title: Launch into very low orbit
milestones.description: Forty-nine spacecraft are deployed near 210 km, where the neutral atmosphere is thin but not negligible and drag is intentionally useful for safe disposal.

milestones.title: Geomagnetic activity rises
milestones.description: Storm energy heats the upper atmosphere. Neutral density at deployment altitude increases even though this is not an extreme geomagnetic storm.

milestones.title: Drag overwhelms climb
milestones.description: The affected spacecraft encounter substantially greater drag than expected and cannot all raise their orbits out of the densest region.

milestones.title: Controlled reentry outcome
milestones.description: Most of the batch reenters without debris reaching the ground. The operational lesson is sensitivity to neutral-density forecasts at very low altitude.

replay.title: Every catalogued member of one launch, drawn from its own element sets

provenance.elements: space-track.org bulk element-set archive for 2022, held on bigmem
provenance.elementsNote: Sean's own space-track account, downloaded once under space-track's instruction to hold the history locally. The series is republished as a derived altitude curve, not as element sets.
provenance.method: Perigee and apogee are derived from the Brouwer mean elements in each published element set: the Kozai mean motion is converted to the semi-major axis with the SGP4 initialisation correction, then a(1-e) and a(1+e) are taken against a spherical Earth of radius 6378.137 km.
provenance.catalogueStart: The catalogue publishes no element sets for the eleven survivors before 8 February, so their traces begin there rather than at launch. The ten that were lost are catalogued from 5-6 February.
provenance.limitation: These are derived orbital altitudes, not measured ranges to the spacecraft, and the catalogue carries 21 of the 49 objects launched. The 28 not shown reentered before a permanent catalogue number was assigned. No point is interpolated: each is one real element set, selected as the nearest to a grid time, carrying its own epoch.

events.title: The Halloween storms of 2003
events.summary: A sequence of exceptionally energetic solar eruptions drove radiation storms and intense geomagnetic activity, disrupted satellites and radio systems, and dramatically reorganized the radiation-belt environment.
events.synopsis: This is the largest set of solar eruptions of the modern instrumented era, and the one that hit the widest range of systems at once. Between 19 October and 7 November 2003 the Sun produced flare after flare from the same few active regions, including the largest X-ray flare ever recorded. Radiation, energetic particles and magnetic storming arrived on three different clocks, which is exactly what the replay is drawn to show: the same event reaching Earth three times, minutes to days apart.
events.lesson: The event demonstrates why a single storm-strength number cannot describe the whole environment: flare radiation, solar energetic particles, magnetospheric currents, and trapped radiation each mattered.

impacts.text: A power system failure in Malmö, southern Sweden, on 30 October left about fifty thousand people without electricity for twenty to thirty minutes. NOAA puts it down to geomagnetically induced currents; the utility said at the time it could not be certain.
impacts.attribution: NOAA service assessment of the October-November 2003 storms

impacts.text: Airlines rerouted more than a dozen flights — some off polar routes altogether — to avoid radiation exposure and the loss of high-frequency radio contact.
impacts.attribution: NOAA service assessment of the October-November 2003 storms

impacts.text: The two-man crew of the International Space Station was directed into the most shielded part of the station, the aft end of the Zvezda service module, for short periods during the worst of the particle storm. NASA put the saving in their exposure at about half.
impacts.attribution: NASA, quoted in the NOAA service assessment of the storms

impacts.text: Satellites were affected across the fleet: instruments were switched off and several spacecraft entered safe mode. Japan's ADEOS-II was lost on 24 October; space weather is suspected in that loss but no official cause was ever established.
impacts.attribution: NOAA service assessment of the October-November 2003 storms, quoting JAXA

impacts.text: A new, temporary radiation belt formed between the two permanent belts.
impacts.attribution: NASA radiation-belt account

impacts.text: The FAA's WAAS augmentation could not be used for precision approaches while the ionosphere was disturbed: its vertical error limit was exceeded for fifteen hours on 29 October and eleven hours on 30 October.
impacts.attribution: NOAA service assessment of the October-November 2003 storms

sources.label: NOAA service assessment of the storms

milestones.title: Major flare sequence
milestones.description: Powerful flares produce immediate radio impacts on the sunlit side and accelerate energetic particles.

milestones.title: Energetic particles arrive
milestones.description: High-energy protons elevate the radiation environment and contaminate some spaceborne sensors.

milestones.title: CME impact
milestones.description: Fast solar-wind plasma and embedded magnetic fields drive severe geomagnetic activity and compress the dayside system.

milestones.title: Radiation belts reorganize
milestones.description: The trapped-particle environment changes in location and intensity. The familiar static two-donut picture is inadequate during a storm.

replay.title: One eruption, three arrivals, three clocks

arrivals.label: Light
arrivals.detail: the X-ray flux lifts off the background
arrivals.note: This one is not a warning. The X-rays and the news of the flare are the same photons, and the ionosphere below them starts absorbing HF the moment they land. The mark sits where the lane lifts off because that is what subtracting the light travel time means — it is arithmetic, not a measurement.

arrivals.label: Flare peak
arrivals.note: The whole of the radio blackout is over before anything else has arrived. By the time an operator has finished diagnosing the HF outage, the particles are still on their way.

arrivals.label: Particles
arrivals.note: Fast enough to be an hour behind the light and slow enough that the hour is usable. This is the window in which a polar route is turned and an EVA is held.

arrivals.label: Particle peak
arrivals.note: An S4 event on NOAA's scale, and still one of the largest handful of proton events in the record NOAA has kept since 1976.

arrivals.label: Field
arrivals.note: The cloud itself, arriving with its magnetic field. Its shock reached Earth at 06:13 UT on 29 October — a Sun-to-Earth transit of about nineteen hours, against an ordinary two to three days. This mark sits a little later, because it is the Dst crossing that follows the shock rather than the shock itself.

arrivals.label: Field minimum
arrivals.note: Two and a half days after the light, and the recovery takes a week. The three clocks never resynchronise.

provenance.xray: GOES-12 X-Ray Sensor, one-minute averages, NOAA NCEI (US Government, public domain).
provenance.protons: GOES-11 Energetic Particle Sensor, five-minute averages, corrected integral channel above 10 MeV, NOAA NCEI.
provenance.dst: Final Dst, World Data Centre for Geomagnetism, Kyoto. Kyoto's terms permit non-commercial use; this site carries no advertising and no paid tier.
provenance.origin: The zero of the axis is the observed X-ray ONSET minus 499.005 seconds, the light travel time over one astronomical unit. Onset is the last minute before the peak at which the 0.1-0.8 nm flux was still below twice the quiet active-region background, which places it at 09:52 UT against NOAA's published 09:51 for this flare. The 499 seconds is the only quantity on this chart that was calculated rather than observed, and the light mark therefore sits where the X-ray lane lifts off by construction rather than by coincidence.
provenance.method: Every plotted point is one real sample, selected as the nearest to a log-spaced grid time and carrying its own timestamp. Nothing is averaged between two measurements and a grid time with no sample near it draws nothing.
provenance.limitation: Three instruments, three cadences, one axis. The X-ray sensor saturates in the largest flares of this same active region — the 4 November event ran off the top of this channel and its class is an extrapolation, which is why the 28 October flare and not the famous one is drawn here. The proton flux is measured at geostationary altitude, inside the magnetosphere, and is not the flux at the top of the atmosphere. No coronagraph data is held, so no CME departure is drawn.

events.title: The Bastille Day event, July 2000
events.summary: An X5.7 flare from a region sitting almost exactly at the centre of the solar disk put a radiation storm at Earth inside the hour and an extreme, G5 geomagnetic storm at Earth a day and a half later. The three arrivals are the same three as the Halloween storms, on a schedule that is not remotely the same.
events.synopsis: This is the event that shows how little warning a radiation storm can give. On 14 July 2000 an X5.7 flare erupted from an active region sitting almost exactly at the centre of the solar disc -- the worst possible place, because it aimed everything at Earth. The radio blackout was immediate, the proton storm began within the hour, and the magnetic storm followed a day later. The replay puts those three arrivals on one clock so the gaps between them are visible.
events.lesson: The interval between the flash and the consequence is not a constant you can look up. Here the protons crossed NOAA's radiation-storm threshold forty minutes after the light, against two hours and twenty-two minutes in 2003, and the field reached its floor at thirty-eight hours against sixty. Both charts are drawn by the same code on the same axis, so the difference is in the storms and not in the drawing.

impacts.text: High-frequency radio on the sunlit side of Earth was blacked out at the moment of the flare.
impacts.attribution: NOAA on the Bastille Day event

impacts.text: Protons crossed NOAA's radiation-storm threshold about forty minutes after the light arrived, giving effectively no warning.
impacts.attribution: GOES-8 proton measurements, NOAA NCEI

impacts.text: Proton damage permanently degraded solar cells: SOHO lost about two percent of its power-generating capacity in a single day, and a transmitter on the Wind spacecraft permanently lost about a quarter of its output.
impacts.attribution: SIDC, Royal Observatory of Belgium, on the Bastille Day event

impacts.text: The ASCA X-ray observatory lost attitude control on 14 July. The heated atmosphere had swollen enough that drag overwhelmed its momentum wheels; it tumbled, its panels came off the Sun, and its batteries ran down. It made no further observations and reentered in March 2001.
impacts.attribution: NASA HEASARC and ISAS mission history

impacts.text: Aurora was reported as far south as Texas and Florida, and into Mexico.
impacts.attribution: Contemporary observer reports collected by Spaceweather.com

sources.label: NOAA on the Bastille Day event
SIDC on the Bastille Day event

milestones.title: Active region 9077 erupts
milestones.description: The 0.1–0.8 nm flux lifts off the background at 10:05 UT; NOAA logs the flare as starting at 10:03. It peaks at 10:24 UT at 5.75e-4 W m⁻², the X5.7 in every account of this day. The region is at the centre of the visible disk, so whatever it throws is aimed at Earth.

milestones.title: Shortwave radio goes out on the daylit side
milestones.description: The X-rays arrive with the news of the flare and ionise the lowest ionosphere, which absorbs HF rather than reflecting it. NOAA records significant disruption to long-range HF communications and a shortwave blackout on the sunlit hemisphere. This project holds no HF measurement for 2000, so the blackout is documented here and not drawn.

milestones.title: The radiation storm starts, with no gap
milestones.description: GOES-8's >10 MeV integral proton channel crosses 10 pfu — NOAA's S1 threshold — at 10:45 UT, while the flare is still brightening. The flux goes on rising for a day to 24,000 pfu, an S4 storm, measured at geostationary altitude.

milestones.title: The shock hits, and the index goes the wrong way
milestones.description: Kyoto's hourly Dst rises to +7 nT at 15 July 15:00 UT. The cloud's leading shock compresses the magnetosphere, and a compressed field read from the ground is a stronger field, so the storm index improves at the moment the storm arrives.

milestones.title: The field reaches its floor
milestones.description: Dst bottoms at −300 nT at 16 July 00:00 UT, thirty-eight hours after the light. NOAA rates the resulting geomagnetic storm G5, the top of its scale. Recovery takes the rest of the week.

replay.title: The same three arrivals, on a completely different schedule

arrivals.label: Light
arrivals.detail: the X-ray flux lifts off the background
arrivals.note: The same arithmetic as the Halloween chart and the same answer, because the speed of light does not care which storm it is. This is the only one of the six marks below whose position was fixed before the event happened.

arrivals.label: Flare peak
arrivals.note: A third the size of the Halloween flare, and it did more damage sooner. Active region 9077 sat almost exactly at the centre of the visible disk, which is the worst geometry for Earth: radiation, particles and cloud were all aimed down the same line at us.

arrivals.label: Particles
arrivals.note: Forty minutes after the light, while the flare was still brightening. On the Halloween chart the same threshold is crossed 2 h 22 min after the light. That gap between the two events is the whole of the usable warning: here there is barely any, and the operator learns about the flare and is already standing in the radiation storm.

arrivals.label: Particle peak
arrivals.note: An S4 event on NOAA's scale. It is the flux, not the flare class, that decides whether a polar route is turned or an EVA is held — and the flux peaked more than a day after the flare itself was over.

arrivals.label: Shock
arrivals.detail: largest Dst in the 12 h before the minimum
arrivals.note: The index goes the WRONG WAY first. A shock arriving at the magnetosphere compresses it, and a compressed field measured from the ground is a STRONGER field, so Dst rises before it falls. Anyone watching one number for 'is it bad yet' sees it improve at the moment the cloud lands.

arrivals.label: Field minimum
arrivals.note: Thirty-eight hours after the light. The Halloween storm took sixty hours to reach its own floor. Same three clocks, twenty-two hours of difference in when the last one strikes, which is why the interval is something you measure every time rather than something you look up.

provenance.xray: GOES-8 X-Ray Sensor, one-minute averages, NOAA NCEI (US Government, public domain). GOES-8 was NOAA's primary spacecraft in July 2000. The archived peak is 5.75e-4 W m⁻²; this page prints X5.8 because it rounds, and NOAA published X5.7 because the class is conventionally truncated. One digit of convention on one measurement — the number in the file is the same either way.
provenance.protons: GOES-8 Energetic Particle Sensor, five-minute averages, corrected integral channel above 10 MeV, NOAA NCEI. The same spacecraft as the X-ray lane above it, which is one fewer cross-calibration to take on trust.
provenance.dst: Final Dst, World Data Centre for Geomagnetism, Kyoto. Kyoto's terms permit non-commercial use; this site carries no advertising and no paid tier.
provenance.origin: The zero of the axis is the observed X-ray ONSET minus 499.005 seconds, the light travel time over one astronomical unit. Onset is the last minute before the peak at which the 0.1-0.8 nm flux was still below twice the quiet active-region background, which places it at 10:05 UT against NOAA's published 10:03 for this flare — two minutes of agreement on a one-minute instrument.
provenance.method: Every plotted point is one real sample, selected as the nearest to a log-spaced grid time and carrying its own timestamp. Nothing is averaged between two measurements and a grid time with no sample near it draws nothing.
provenance.limitation: The two Dst marks here are extrema over stated windows, not threshold crossings. The 'crosses −50 nT' rule the Halloween chart uses fires seven hours early on this storm, on a small separate disturbance that recovered inside the hour, so it is not used and no per-event threshold was invented to replace it. As on the other chart, the proton flux is measured at geostationary altitude, inside the magnetosphere, and is not the flux at the top of the atmosphere; no coronagraph data is held, so no CME departure is drawn.

events.title: The St Patrick's Day storm, March 2015
events.summary: The largest geomagnetic storm of its solar cycle came from a modest C-class flare and an unremarkable coronal mass ejection. What made it severe was the direction of the magnetic field the cloud was carrying, and the solar wind was still speeding up a full day after the storm had passed its worst.
events.synopsis: This is the storm that proves severity is not set by the size of the flare. The largest geomagnetic storm of its entire solar cycle came from an unremarkable C-class flare and an ordinary coronal mass ejection on 17 March 2015. What made it severe was the direction of the magnetic field it carried: it arrived pointing south, which is the one orientation that lets energy into the magnetosphere. The replay follows that field direction and the ring current filling behind it.
events.lesson: Cause and effect are separated here, in view, in the right order. The arriving field turns south, the ring current takes nine hours and forty minutes to fill, and the quantity that looks most like a cause — speed — peaks a day after the storm bottomed out. This is the case that shows why a forecast cannot be made from how fast something is coming.

impacts.text: The storm reached G4 (severe) and was the largest of solar cycle 24, bottoming at Dst −223 nT.
impacts.attribution: NOAA SWPC for the G4 rating; published analyses of the storm for the cycle ranking

impacts.text: Aurora was seen at mid-latitudes in both hemispheres, from New Zealand to Alaska and as far south as the central and southern United States.
impacts.attribution: NASA Earth Observatory

impacts.text: High-frequency radio and single-frequency GPS positioning were degraded while the ionosphere was disturbed.
impacts.attribution: NOAA SWPC storm-scale effects; published GNSS positioning studies of this storm

sources.label: NOAA SWPC on the G4 storm
NASA Earth Observatory: the aurora, up and down

milestones.title: A quiet field, and a cloud already on its way
milestones.description: The window opens with the interplanetary field near zero and the wind near 300 km/s. The coronal mass ejection that will arrive was launched on 15 March with a C9.1 flare — nothing about the eruption marked it as the storm of the cycle.

milestones.title: The shock arrives and the index goes UP
milestones.description: SYM/H reaches +67 nT at 04:48 UT on 17 March, its highest value in the window. The shock compresses the magnetosphere and a compressed field read from the ground is a stronger one, so the storm index improves at the moment the storm lands. Measured, one-minute SYM/H, carried in the NASA OMNI record.

milestones.title: The field turns south, hard
milestones.description: Bz in GSM reaches −26.0 nT at 13:07 UT. The arriving field is now antiparallel to Earth's on the dayside, the two can reconnect, and energy starts going in. Measured at L1 by ACE and Wind and time-shifted to the bow shock nose by OMNI.

milestones.title: The ring current finishes filling
milestones.description: SYM/H bottoms at −234 nT at 22:47 UT, nine hours and forty minutes after the field turned south, because the ring current is an accumulation rather than a reading. NOAA rated the storm G4, severe; the aurora was seen from the central and southern United States.

milestones.title: The wind is at its fastest, and it no longer matters
milestones.description: Flow speed peaks at 692 km/s at 23:32 UT on 18 March, almost twenty-five hours after the storm floor, with the index already well into recovery. If speed were the driver the worst of this storm would be here.

replay.title: A fast wind does nothing until the field turns south

lanes.label: IMF Bz (GSM)
lanes.instrument: ACE and Wind at L1, one-minute, time-shifted to the bow shock nose by NASA OMNI

lanes.label: Solar-wind speed
lanes.instrument: ACE and Wind plasma instruments, one-minute, same OMNI time shift

lanes.label: SYM/H
lanes.instrument: SYM/H, one-minute, Kyoto WDC, carried in the OMNI record

marks.label: Shock
marks.detail: SYM/H at its maximum in the window
marks.note: The cloud's leading shock squeezes the magnetosphere inward, and a compressed field measured from the ground is a STRONGER field. The storm index therefore goes up at the moment the storm arrives. Nothing has gone in yet.

marks.label: Field turns south
marks.note: Now the arriving field is antiparallel to Earth's at the dayside and the two can reconnect. This is the moment energy starts going in, and it is the only quantity on this chart whose sign decides whether there is a storm at all.

marks.label: Storm floor
marks.note: 9.7 hours after the field turned south. The ring current is an accumulation, not a reading: it keeps deepening for as long as the door is open, so the worst moment is hours after the cause that made it.

marks.label: Fastest wind
marks.note: 25 hours AFTER the storm bottomed out, with the index already recovering. If speed were the thing that mattered the worst of this storm would be here, at the right-hand edge, and it is not.

provenance.field: Interplanetary magnetic field Bz in GSM coordinates and solar-wind flow speed, one-minute, from the High Resolution OMNI data set. The OMNI data were obtained from the GSFC/SPDF OMNIWeb interface at https://omniweb.gsfc.nasa.gov. The upstream measurements in this window are ACE (magnetic field: Smith; plasma: McComas) and Wind (magnetic field: Lepping; plasma: Ogilvie).
provenance.symh: SYM/H, the one-minute longitudinally symmetric disturbance index, produced by the World Data Centre for Geomagnetism, Kyoto, and carried inside the OMNI record. It is NOT Dst: Dst is hourly and built from a different station set. Papers on this storm quote a minimum Dst of −223 nT; the one-minute SYM/H minimum drawn here is −234 nT. Both are right, and this page says which it is.
provenance.shift: The top two lanes are measured about 1.5 million km upstream at the first Lagrange point, not at Earth. OMNI time-shifts each one-minute average forward to the nose of Earth's bow shock using the measured flow and the observed orientation of the field's phase front. That shift — half an hour to an hour at these speeds — is the only derived quantity on this chart.
provenance.method: Ten-minute bins. Each record is the real sample nearest the bin centre, carrying its own timestamp, plus the smallest and largest real sample inside the bin, which the chart draws as the band. Nothing is averaged and nothing is interpolated; a bin with no valid sample produces no record, so a gap in the archive is drawn as a gap. Values are published to 0.1 nT for the field and to 1 unit for the speed and the index — in each case a small fraction of one pixel on the lane that draws them.
provenance.licence: OMNI is a NASA product and is freely available; NASA asks that its use be acknowledged in the wording carried above, and that the principal investigators who supplied the upstream data be credited, which is why they are named rather than summarised as 'L1 monitors'.
provenance.limitation: Bz here is what the field did UPSTREAM. How much of it actually got in depends on the reconnection rate, which nobody measures directly, so this chart shows the cause and the consequence and does not draw the coupling between them. The plasma instruments are also incomplete over this window and the gaps are left empty; the magnetic field and SYM/H lanes are nearly continuous. Finally, one storm cannot prove a rule: it is a clean, large, well-measured demonstration of a relationship established over decades of events, not the evidence for it.

events.title: The March 1989 Québec blackout storm
events.summary: A severe geomagnetic storm induced currents in long conductors and contributed to the collapse of Hydro-Québec's transmission system, producing a nine-hour blackout.
events.synopsis: This is the storm that took a power grid down. A severe geomagnetic storm on 13 March 1989 drove rapid changes in Earth's magnetic field over eastern Canada, and those changes induced currents in the long conductors of Hydro-Quebec's transmission system. The grid went from normal to collapsed in about ninety seconds. What you are about to watch is that chain drawn in order, from the field change on the ground to the protective relays tripping.
events.lesson: This case extends the chain all the way to the ground: magnetospheric and ionospheric currents change Earth's magnetic field, which can induce electric fields and currents in infrastructure.

impacts.text: A static compensator tripped at 02:44:17 EST and the Québec grid separated ninety-two seconds later, leaving about six million people without power for more than nine hours.
impacts.attribution: Hydro-Québec's account of the collapse and the North American Electric Reliability Council review

impacts.text: Aurora was reported unusually far south — as far as Florida and Cuba.
impacts.attribution: Contemporary reports summarised by NASA

impacts.text: Induced currents caused substantial interference in United States power grids and damaged a high-voltage transformer at a nuclear plant in New Jersey.
impacts.attribution: USGS geomagnetic hazard literature

impacts.text: Shortwave radio was disrupted, including the signals Radio Free Europe was broadcasting into Russia, and some satellites tumbled out of control for several hours.
impacts.attribution: NASA, "The Day the Sun Brought Darkness" (2009)

milestones.title: Interplanetary shock
milestones.description: The solar-wind disturbance reaches Earth and initiates a severe magnetospheric response.

milestones.title: Rapid field changes
milestones.description: Strong current systems produce rapid magnetic variations at the ground, inducing geoelectric fields in conductive Earth.

milestones.title: Grid collapse
milestones.description: Geomagnetically induced currents contribute to protection-system trips and the Québec grid collapses in under two minutes.

milestones.title: Infrastructure recovery
milestones.description: Power is restored over hours while the geospace system continues to evolve. The reconstruction does not imply modern global measurements existed in 1989.

video.caption: The chain, drawn: a field that moves, an electric field in the rock, a current up a transformer neutral, a core saturating on half of every cycle, the harmonics that makes, and the relays that answered them. Rendered with Manim; narrated in Sean's own voice from a written script.

transcript.text: A hundred kilometres up, a sheet of current the width of a continent shifts south and strengthens. At Ottawa the magnetic field moved four hundred and thirty five nanotesla in one minute. On a quiet night it moves one.
A magnetic field that changes drives an electric field in the rock beneath it. Faraday's law has a time derivative in it, so what matters is the rate and not the depth. A few volts per kilometre.

Both ends of a long transmission line are bolted to the ground through a transformer neutral. Multiply a few volts per kilometre by a few hundred kilometres, and current flows up one neutral, along the line, and down the other.

That current is nearly direct, and a core built for sixty hertz has no answer to it. The offset pushes half of every cycle over the knee, where a small change in flux costs an enormous magnetising current.

The current stops being a sine wave and becomes a spike. A spike is a stack of harmonics the network was tuned to exclude, and the flux that no longer fits inside the core goes into the steel around it as heat.
The protective relays saw distortion they were built to disconnect for, and they disconnected. Seven compensators tripped one after another, inside a minute.
Five lines opened and the La Grande corridor was gone. Ninety two seconds later so was Quebec. Twenty one thousand five hundred megawatts, six million people, nine hours.

provenance.rate: Ottawa magnetic observatory, operated by the Geological Survey of Canada (Natural Resources Canada). Definitive one-minute X and Y, obtained from the World Data Centre for Geomagnetism, Edinburgh. Published here only as a derived rate curve, on the same non-commercial footing this project already applies to INTERMAGNET and to Kyoto: fine for a non-profit teaching site, and the first thing to re-source if that ever changes.
provenance.index: Final hourly Dst, World Data Centre for Geomagnetism, Kyoto. Non-commercial use; this site carries no advertising and no paid tier.
provenance.method: Each point is the magnitude of the change in the horizontal field between two consecutive one-minute samples, √(ΔX² + ΔY²). Nothing is smoothed, and a minute whose predecessor is missing draws nothing rather than a rate across a gap.
provenance.blackoutTime: 02:44:17 EST on 13 March 1989, from Hydro-Québec's account of the separation and the subsequent North American Electric Reliability Council review. It is a reported wall-clock time, not something measured here.
provenance.limitation: This is the rate at Ottawa, not at La Grande, and the currents that mattered flowed a thousand kilometres further north through very old, very resistive Canadian Shield rock. It is also not the largest rate of the storm: Ottawa saw 556 nT/min the following morning with no second collapse. Rate is the right quantity to watch and it is not by itself sufficient — the state of the network when the rate arrives matters as much. Nothing here is a measurement of a geomagnetically induced current, because none was being made in Québec that night.
provenance.animation: The mechanism panel is a drawn schematic, rendered with Manim from the sequence described in the published post-mortems. It is a labelled diagram of a causal chain, not a recording of one, and no part of it is footage.
